newsitem.title: USA: Dole lashes Clinton ethics, president braces for nasty debate.
newsitem.headline: Dole lashes Clinton ethics, president braces for nasty debate.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent

Republican candidate Bob Dole on Tuesday warmed up for the final presidential debate with a fierce attack on President Bill Clinton's ethical standards, but the president dismissed the onslaught as "just politics."

With polls showing he risks a big defeat in the Nov. 5 election, Dole has apparently decided he has little to lose by going after Clinton in the 90-minute "Town Hall Meeting" on Wednesday in San Diego, when the two candidates will answer questions from an audience of some 150 undecided voters.

"No administration has been more self-righteous," Dole told a business group luncheon. "But few administrations have been more self-serving. No administration has shown more arrogance. But few have displayed more ethical failures."

For months, Dole was clearly hesitant to take off the gloves, fearing the tactic would rebound against him by reminding voters of his image for harshness. He has ruled out personal attacks against the president, but now seems prepared to focus on some of the various legal probes being carried out against members of the Clinton administration.

"Among members of this administration there is a growing gap -- an integrity gap -- between the low standards they have adopted and the high honor that they hold," Dole told the San Diego Electronic Industrial Association luncheon.
"A gap between their swagger and their public scandals. A gap between what the presidency itself has been, and what it has lately and sadly become," he said.

Clinton spent the day practicing for the debate at a retreat in Albuquerque, New Mexico, obviously rehearsing his responses to the anticipated Dole onslaught. Former Senate Democratic Leader George Mitchell was playing the part of Dole in the practice sessions and was not pulling any punches.
"This may turn nasty," a senior campaign official said. "We're certainly getting ready for it."
Emerging to take some reporters' questions, Clinton gave a foretaste of what his response is likely to be in San Diego.
"Senator Dole takes the position that if it's good, I didn't have anything to do with it and if it's bad, I must have stayed up all night planning it," he said. "That's just politics."

Asked about Dole's attacks on his ethics, Clinton said: "He's been doing a lot of that and I'll have a chance to answer that at the appropriate time ... My view is this country is better off than it was four years ago and we have worked hard to make it so. And we've worked hard by concentrating on ideas and issues, not insults."

A late-breaking flurry of charges about questionable financial contributions to the Democratic Party and the Clinton administration by Asian businessmen has provided the Dole camp with new ammunition to fire at the president.

"And now we see new charges that this administration has allowed a wealthy Indonesian family to buy presidential access, and play a role in foreign policy, in exchange for contributions to the Democratic National Committee," Dole said.
Dole's vice presidential running mate Jack Kemp charged on Tuesday the contributions had been channeled in such a way as to avoid U.S. limits on foreign contributions.

A television audience of 70 million may tune in for the debate, which is seen by the Clinton camp as the last major obstacle the president must surmount on his way to election victory. The town hall meeting format is considered Clinton's great strength and may make it difficult for Dole to launch sharp attacks. In any case, past debates have rarely radically altered the course of a presidential campaign.
White House Political Director Doug Sosnik said a negative approach by Dole would only cost him votes on Election Day, with Reform Party candidate Ross Perot the beneficiary.

There were some signs of that in the latest Reuters daily tracking poll, which showed Clinton lengthening his lead above 15 percentage points. It was the eighth consecutive day the president had extended his advantage.
